annotation.title: Organizing pneumonia secondary to Pneumocystis jirovecii infection in a kidney transplant recipient: Case report and review of literature

cases.case_text:
A 36-year-old man with end-stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy underwent a live-related renal transplant 6 months ago and has been maintained on tacrolimus 3.5 mg daily, mycophenolate sodium 720 mg daily, and prednisolone 7.5 mg daily. He presented with a 14-day history of low-grade fever, dry cough, and anorexia without dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, or weight loss. He was afebrile on admission, heart rate 88 beats/min, blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Examination revealed bilateral inspiratory crackles; other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL; total lymphocyte count 9900/μL; absolute neutrophil count 7720/μL; platelets 285 000/μL; serum creatinine 1.05 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated PaO₂ 68 mm Hg and an A–a gradient of 22 mm Hg. HIV ELISA was negative. Chest radiograph revealed bilateral diffuse alveolar infiltrates. High-resolution CT of the chest showed bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities without pleural or mediastinal abnormalities.

Sputum induction was non-diagnostic. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii on Grocott’s methenamine silver stain and negative for acid-fast bacilli, CMV inclusion bodies, and fungal hyphae. He was treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and a prednisone taper, with clinical and radiographic resolution of infiltrates after 2 weeks.

Three weeks into therapy, he was asymptomatic except for an occasional dry cough. TMP-SMX was discontinued, and prednisolone was maintained at 10 mg daily. Laboratory studies then showed leukopenia (TLC 1400/μL; ANC 1050/μL). Chest radiograph revealed new left upper-zone infiltrates. Repeat HRCT showed resolution of ground-glass opacities and new patchy peribronchovascular consolidations in the right upper lobe, left upper lobe, and left lower-lobe apical segment. Repeat BAL was negative for AFB, fungus, and Pneumocystis jirovecii. 

Transbronchial lung biopsy from the left upper lobe showed alveoli filled with inflammatory debris consisting of granulation tissue, interstitial inflammation, and areas of intra-alveolar fibrin deposition.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Organizing pneumonia
B. Persistent or recrudescent PCP is unlikely
C. Cytomegalovirus pneumonia was excluded
D. Atypical bacterial pneumonia was considered but not supported
E. Tacrolimus
F. Organizing pneumonia was supported by histopathology and timing
G. Secondary (postinfectious) OP related to PCP was favored over cryptogenic OP
H. None

annotation.title: Toxocara Myopericarditis and Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging in a Young Girl

cases.case_text:
A 9-year-old girl with a small muscular ventricular septal defect presented with chest pain and dyspnea one week after recovering from an upper respiratory infection and after minor anterior chest trauma in a fall. She was afebrile. Heart rate was 104 beats/min, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, blood pressure 113/66 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation normal. Physical examination revealed mild tenderness over the sternum and normal cardiac auscultation. 

Chest radiography showed mild cardiomediastinal silhouette enlargement and a focal opacity in the right middle lung. ECG was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion with right atrial collapse, normal biventricular systolic function, and no ventricular septal defect. 

Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 12,000 cells/µL with an absolute eosinophil count of 1,570 cells/µL (normal 40–190), C-reactive protein 1.94 mg/dL (normal <0.5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 45 mm/hr (normal 0–30), and troponin T 0.25 ng/mL (normal <0.1). Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed elevated global myocardial T2 (70 ms) and T1 (1150 ms) values, increased left ventricular wall thickness, a moderate pericardial effusion, and no late gadolinium enhancement.

She was admitted with a working diagnosis of viral myopericarditis. Treatment with oral ibuprofen and colchicine resulted in resolution of chest pain, normalization of troponin and inflammatory markers, and reduction of the pericardial effusion over three days. However, the absolute eosinophil count rose further. Consultations with infectious diseases, allergy/immunology, and rheumatology were obtained. Further history elicited pica and exposure to two dogs and a cat. 

Chest computed tomography revealed multiple pulmonary nodules with adjacent ground-glass opacities. An infectious workup showed negative PCR tests for influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus, rhinovirus, and adenovirus; negative Bartonella henselae titers; and a negative T-SPOT tuberculosis test. Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM and IgG were elevated, but nasopharyngeal Mycoplasma PCR was negative. Toxocara serology was sent and was pending at discharge.

annotation.title: Twin anemia polycythemia sequence in dichorionic diamniotic twins: A case report and review of the literature

cases.case_text:
A 34-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman with a spontaneous dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy was transferred at 31 weeks 5 days’ gestation. Dichorionicity had been confirmed on first-trimester ultrasound. Pregnancy complications included early-onset growth restriction in twin 2 and new-onset preeclampsia at 30 weeks. At 16 weeks, ultrasound showed twin 1 with normal growth and normal amniotic fluid; twin 2 had estimated fetal weight <5th percentile, anhydramnios, and an absent bladder. Confirmatory ultrasound at 19 weeks revealed Tetralogy of Fallot in twin 2. By 21 weeks, twin 2’s amniotic fluid improved from anhydramnios to oligohydramnios (maximum vertical pocket 1.9 cm), and later normalized in both twins. Invasive testing was declined initially; at 31 weeks, chorionic villus sampling of twin 2 showed a normal chromosomal microarray.  
At 32 weeks, ultrasound at the tertiary center demonstrated:  
• Twin 1: estimated fetal weight 1904 g (62nd centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) 26 cm/s (0.56 multiples of the mean).  
• Twin 2: estimated fetal weight 1128 g (<5th centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and MCA-PSV 50.9 cm/s (1.3 MoM).  
Placental imaging showed a normal-appearing placenta for twin 1 and a thickened, echogenic placenta for twin 2. These findings prompted suspicion for twin anemia-polycythemia sequence and an emergency cesarean section at 32 + 2 weeks.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. twin anemia polycythemia sequence
B. Considered twin
C. Considered genetic or chromosomal cause of growth restriction
D. Evaluated standard antenatal ISUOG criteria for TAPS
E. Applied proposed delta MCA
F. Assessed postnatal hemoglobin difference for TAPS confirmation
G. Noted absence of required postnatal reticulocyte ratio or dye studies for formal confirmation
H. None

cases.case_text:
A 13-year-old girl from a hilly region of Nepal presented with intermittent fever with chills and profuse sweating for 1 month. The fever was low grade, occurring at intervals, and associated with lassitude and dry cough. She had received courses of antibiotics and antipyretics without improvement. She had no travel history to leishmaniasis‐endemic areas. On examination, she appeared pale and ill; temperature was 99.4°F, respiratory rate was increased, and heart rate was elevated. Oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. There was no icterus, lymphadenopathy, cyanosis, clubbing, edema, or sternal tenderness. Abdominal examination revealed massive splenomegaly extending to the umbilical line and mild hepatomegaly, with the liver palpable two fingers below the right midclavicular line. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.2 g/dL, total leukocyte count 3150/µL, and absolute neutrophil count 1386/µL. Blood glucose and electrolytes were normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 46 mm/h, and C-reactive protein was reactive. Liver enzymes were elevated with ALT 130 U/L and AST 143 U/L. A chest radiograph and electrocardiogram were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed gross hepatosplenomegaly with a liver span of 16.2 cm and spleen span of 18.1 cm.

annotation.title: Tuberculous hemorrhagic meningoencephalitis. A rare manifestation of miliary TB. Case report and review

cases.case_text:
A 39-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of persistent fever, night sweats, a 15-kg weight loss, decreased appetite, dry cough, and shortness of breath. He had no significant medical history, no recent travel, and no known sick contacts, but lived in close quarters with 13 other inmates. On examination, his heart rate was elevated, blood pressure was low but responsive to fluids, and he had fine tremors. Laboratory studies showed hyponatremia, elevated liver enzymes (AST, ALT, ALP), and raised inflammatory markers. Anteroposterior chest radiography revealed numerous bilateral tiny nodules throughout both lung fields. Contrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirmed innumerable widespread pulmonary nodules, a few cavitary lesions, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Because of his headache, an MRI of the brain was obtained, which demonstrated vasogenic edema in the left posterior insula and temporoparietal cortex, intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the same region, and overlying leptomeningeal enhancement—findings consistent with hemorrhagic meningoencephalitis.

cases.case_text:

• Serum calcium 3.8 mmol/L (normal phosphorus), nonregenerative normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 9 g/dL), and acute functional renal failure (creatinine clearance 30 mL/min).  
• PTH 9 ng/L.  
• Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia; negative 24-hour proteinuria; no monoclonal peak on serum or urine immunoelectrophoresis; normal serum free light-chain ratio.  

She received IV saline and one dose of zoledronate, with normalization of calcium and renal function by day 3. A CT scan of the body showed two osteolytic lesions of the left frontal and temporal skull bones, multiple hypodense micronodules in all hepatic segments, and multiple splenic nodules. Brain MRI demonstrated T2-hyperintense, T1-isointense, gadolinium-enhancing lesions in the same skull regions. A DEXA scan revealed osteopenia (lumbar spine T-score –2.4). Mammography, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal. Bone marrow biopsy and labial salivary gland histology were unremarkable. A percutaneous fine-needle aspiration of the liver showed noncaseating granulomatous hepatitis without malignancy. The intradermal tuberculin test was negative. cases.case_text:
A 55-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and opioid use disorder presented with worsening abdominal distention and a 60-lb unintentional weight loss over 1 year, along with increasing difficulty with bowel movements. He denied melena, nausea, vomiting, fevers, flank pain, dysphagia, or odynophagia, and had no history of abdominal surgery.

Three weeks before admission, abdominal CT with contrast showed a small-bowel obstruction with a transition point in the right-mid abdomen and focal small-bowel wall thickening, plus mesenteric adenopathy. His symptoms improved without intervention, and he was discharged.

He returned 3 weeks later with diffuse abdominal pain. Repeat CT showed multiple dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels. Colonoscopy revealed two polyps; cold-forceps biopsies showed non-specific chronic inflammation without features of inflammatory bowel disease. Video capsule endoscopy demonstrated erythematous gastritis, multiple small-bowel ulcers, and an atrophic duodenum. Two weeks later, double-balloon enteroscopy identified multiple jejunal strictures and areas suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease, and outpatient IBD management was planned.

Two months later, he presented with severe abdominal pain, new nausea, and vomiting. Abdominal radiographs suggested pneumoperitoneum. Exploratory laparotomy revealed a perforated ulcer in the terminal ileum, which was repaired, and a proximal Brooke ileostomy was created. Biopsies around the perforation showed ulcerated mucosa with non-specific chronic inflammation. He was discharged after a 21-day hospital stay.

One month later, he was re-hospitalized for non-specific abdominal symptoms and increased ostomy output. Ileoscopy showed scalloped mucosa with blunted villi throughout the ileum, and biopsies were taken. Histologic examination revealed extensive lymphocytic infiltrates with epitheliotropism but no definitive atypical morphological features, raising suspicion for a lymphoid neoplasm. cases.case_text:
A 51-year-old woman noticed a 2-cm palpable right-breast lump in 2019 that grew progressively. By June 2021 the overlying skin ulcerated with straw-colored exudate. She had local pain but no systemic symptoms. She had no chronic medical history. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 83 g/L) and slightly low albumin; other blood counts and liver function tests were near normal. Breast ultrasound revealed loss of normal architecture with mixed cystic (>90%) and solid echoes. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI demonstrated a large irregular cystic-solid lesion with internal fluid levels and tortuous vessels; a right axillary lymph node showed slight cortical thickening. cases.case_text:
A 75-year-old woman, previously well, transferred her care to a new general practitioner in June 2022. She reported a presumed stroke in April 2020 with slurred speech, imbalance, and confusion lasting 48 hours; at that time, brain MRI showed chronic periventricular white matter changes without acute ischemic lesions, and CT angiography demonstrated carotid tortuosity with stenosis from myointimal plaques. Her medications included barnidipine 20 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg daily.

Since 2020, she experienced recurrent dizzying attacks characterized by sudden subjective vertigo, absence of nausea or vomiting, and unsteadiness with a wide-based gait requiring support; episodes lasted days to weeks and gradually resolved. Symptomatic treatments for dizziness were ineffective. Over months, attacks increased in frequency and duration until dizziness became constant, leading to loss of autonomy.

At the first visit, general and neurologic examinations were normal, and she reported a low mood. Days later, a severe attack prevented her from getting out of bed, prompting a home visit. Vital signs were normal; she was alert, oriented, and cooperative with normal speech. She described severe dizziness worsened by any movement or position change, without nausea or vomiting. With assistance, she sat on the bed with difficulty maintaining trunk control. When upright, she adopted a wide-based stance, was unsteady, and required external supports to walk. Romberg’s test was positive, with marked unsteadiness on eye closure. Strength and sensation were intact, reflexes were normal, and cranial nerves were intact. The finger–nose test was weakly positive on the right. The HINTS examination was negative.

A diagnostic algorithm for dizziness suggested a low probability of central or peripheral vestibular origin. Review of the CTA suggested that carotid stenosis had been overestimated due to marked vessel tortuosity. annotation.title: Metastatic hemangiosarcoma of the liver in a young rat

cases.case_text:
A 3-week-old male Sprague-Dawley rat was housed under standard conditions and assigned to a control group in a pharmacological study. At 7 weeks of age, the rat appeared clinically normal and was euthanized under anesthesia. At necropsy, the liver and other organs appeared grossly unremarkable, and serum AST and ALT levels were within normal limits.

A sample from the left lateral liver lobe was fixed in formalin, embedded, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin, Azan, and Watanabe’s silver stain. Histologically, there were multifocal basophilic foci located predominantly in the perilobular region. Within these foci, polygonal to short spindle-shaped cells formed small nests and sheets within dilated sinusoids without encapsulation. The tumor cells exhibited clear cell borders, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, hyperchromatic nuclei, frequent mitotic figures, and sparse hepatocellular necrosis. A 45-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of an abrupt onset of an asymptomatic cutaneous eruption on the neck and both forearms. On examination, there were multiple papules and plaques of varying sizes on the dorsal forearms and nape of the neck, each showing a striking central depression that mimicked vesiculation; some neck lesions had an overlying crust. All lesions were firm and nontender.

annotation.title: Focal epilepsy presenting as a bath-induced paroxysmal event/breath-holding attack

cases.case_text:
A 19-month-old boy was brought to the emergency department after an episode of reduced consciousness while bathing. His parents reported that when lukewarm water was poured over his chest, he turned blue around the lips and began gasping for air. During this time, his eyes “rolled back,” and he did not interact with his parents. There were no clonic movements, and he did not respond to physical stimulation. He subsequently fell asleep for approximately 1 hour and was brought to the ED.

On arrival, he was alert and appeared well. There were no focal findings on examination, his development was appropriate, and laboratory studies—including a blood glucose level of 5.5 mmol/L—were normal. His parents reported similar, less profound episodes during bathing over the previous 2 weeks, in which his head would go back, his eyes would roll upward, and he would become floppy and limp for 2–3 minutes, followed by sleepiness. These episodes occurred only during bathing; contact with water in other settings did not provoke symptoms. He had normal developmental milestones and no significant past medical or family history.

An electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm with a normal QT interval. Bathing in lukewarm water while his vital signs were monitored provoked hypotonia, tachycardia, and brief apnea with associated desaturation. He stared straight ahead and made mouthing movements; he was removed from the bath, given high-flow oxygen, and again slept for about 1 hour. A further similar episode occurred later while he was sleeping, without any provocation. The first interictal EEG was normal using the standard 10–20 system. Because he was clinically well between episodes and there was an avoidable trigger, he was discharged with plans for follow-up investigations, including a brain MRI, a bathing EEG, and outpatient review.

annotation.title: Metastatic extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma presenting as a forehead mass

cases.case_text:
A man in his mid-30s was referred for further management of a forehead mass initially thought to be a lipoma. The lesion had appeared 1 year earlier after minor forehead trauma and had slowly enlarged over the past 4 months without pain or other symptoms. His history was notable for extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma of the left foot treated 9 years earlier with below‐knee amputation and adjuvant ifosfamide–doxorubicin chemotherapy.

On examination, there was a 10 cm × 8 cm soft, compressible mass on the right forehead extending from the hairline to the mid‐forehead. In the operating suite, a full‐thickness skin and frontalis incision exposed a gray, well‐circumscribed mass. A palpable bony step‐off at the base prompted aborting resection and closing the incision.

Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a mass arising from the right frontal diploic space with intracranial extension and possible involvement of the superior sagittal sinus. Noncontrast head CT revealed a lytic lesion of the right frontal bone with hypodense soft‐tissue extension into the scalp.

cases.case_text:
A 34-year-old North African woman with no significant past medical history was referred for management of obstructive jaundice. Two months earlier, she had undergone laparotomy and resection of the protruding dome of a segment I hepatic cyst thought to be a hydatid cyst compressing the biliary convergence. She now presented with fever to 38.5 °C, mucocutaneous jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools. On examination, she was febrile and icteric; there was no abdominal tenderness, hepatomegaly, or palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed moderate hepatocellular enzyme elevations and cholestasis. cases.case_text:
An 83-year-old man presented with 6 months of progressive right mandibular pain radiating to the zygomatic and mastoid regions, requiring oxycodone, paracetamol, and ketorolac for relief. An empirical course of prednisone (50 mg per day) for presumed trigeminal neuralgia provided no benefit. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial CT showed enlargement of the right sphenoid sinus with overdevelopment and opacity of the lateral recess, bone thickening and sclerosis of the sphenoid walls, pterygoid process, and orbital apex, and focal interruption of the foramen rotundum and lateral recess wall. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI demonstrated soft tissue protruding through a breach in the lateral recess wall of the sphenoid sinus, invading the right internal pterygoid muscles, masticatory and pterygopalatine fossae, and infiltrating the V2 and V3 trigeminal branches; intracranial extension into the cavernous sinus surrounded the Gasserian ganglion, with the cavernous carotid artery patent. T2-weighted images showed a markedly hypointense signal in the lateral recess with peripheral mucosal inflammation. Endoscopic evaluation revealed purulent discharge in the sphenoethmoidal recess. The patient underwent right endoscopic sinus surgery: after middle turbinectomy, the sphenoid ostium was obstructed by a pyocele, which was marsupialized and drained; samples of the lesion and surrounding mucosa were sent for bacteriological and histopathological examination. The maxillary and ethmoid sinuses were then opened, the breach in the posterior-lateral sphenoid wall was repaired with mucoperiosteum, and a Merocel sponge was placed. He was discharged after 2 days without complications. Histopathology was negative for hyphae and neoplastic cells, and cultures grew no bacteria or fungi. annotation.title: An adolescent girl with signs and symptoms of anaphylaxis and negative immunologic workup: a case report

cases.case_text:
A 14-year-old Caucasian girl was transferred from a community emergency department after treatment for presumed anaphylaxis following ingestion of a hypoallergenic nutritional supplement. Immediately after ingestion she reported wheezing, cough, and swelling of the lips, face, and tongue and self-administered epinephrine (0.3 mg) at home. Her history included suspected food allergies (wheat, oats, tree nuts, chocolate, eggs, cow’s milk, and rice) without documented reactions; intermittent asthma; complex regional pain syndrome; delayed gastric emptying; and major depressive disorder treated with fluoxetine, increased to 60 mg daily 5 months earlier. Skin prick tests and serum-specific IgE to foods of concern were negative except for sensitization to several tree nuts without a supportive history of reaction with ingestion. Testing for hereditary angioedema and baseline serum tryptase were normal. She had lost 40 lb over the past year through dietary restriction and exercise and was homeschooled due to fears of allergic reactions.

In the ED she had stridor, biphasic wheezing, and poor air movement without visible oropharyngeal swelling. She was afebrile, blood pressure 94/48 mmHg, heart rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 30/min, and SpO₂ 100% on room air. She received IV fluids, two doses of subcutaneous epinephrine, inhaled bronchodilators, racemic epinephrine, and antihistamines, and was admitted to the PICU. Her presumed angioedema resolved with treatment.

Over the next several weeks in an eating-disorder program, she had seven similar episodes requiring ED evaluation and PICU admission. Each episode featured subjective perioral swelling, hypotension within her baseline range, and stridor that resolved without objective edema. Direct laryngoscopy during one episode showed no airway edema or paradoxical vocal cord motion. Serial serum tryptase levels during acute events remained normal, a bone marrow biopsy was equivocal, and further workup—including complement levels, mast cell mediators, urine prostaglandins, complete blood count, and metabolic panel—was unremarkable. She was managed with daily antihistamines, ranitidine, cromolyn, and a tapering course of prednisone; rescue therapy included cetirizine and lorazepam. She continued to experience suicidal ideation and auditory hallucinations and was started on aripiprazole.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Factitious disorder
B. IgE
C. True anaphylaxis was less likely
D. Mast cell activation syndrome (mastocytosis) was excluded
E. Hereditary angioedema was ruled out
F. Vocal cord dysfunction was not found
G. Fluoxetine

annotation.title: Cesarean section scar ectopic pregnancy - a management conundrum: a case report

cases.case_text:
A 36-year-old G5P2+2 woman with two prior cesarean deliveries and two first-trimester miscarriages was referred at 6 weeks of amenorrhea for evaluation of a pregnancy of unknown location. Her serum quantitative β-hCG was 16,124 mIU/mL. A transabdominal ultrasound at presentation did not locate an intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy. A copper intrauterine device had been removed 2 months before her last menstrual period. She had used one cycle of clomiphene. She had no chronic illnesses, did not smoke or drink, and was not on medications.

On examination, blood pressure was 113/70 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min, and temperature 37.5 °C. Abdominal, cardiorespiratory, neurological, and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 13 mm gestational sac with irregular margins and a yolk sac in the anterior isthmic portion of the uterus, raising suspicion for a cesarean-section scar ectopic pregnancy. Doppler was declined. Serial β-hCG measurements rose by 33% over 48 hours (21,521 mIU/mL). The patient missed follow-up and returned 1 week later with 5 days of worsening pelvic pain.

Repeat transvaginal scan revealed a fetal pole with cardiac activity (crown–rump length 0.9 cm) in a sac traversing the full width of the anterior myometrium, extending exophytically toward the serosa, with trophoblastic flow on Doppler; there was no endometrial fluid or free pelvic fluid. She was taken to laparoscopy and hysteroscopy: the bladder was densely adherent to the anterior uterine wall, the ectopic was not visualized, and extensive intrauterine adhesions obscured the view; there was no intracavitary bleeding. Postoperatively, she became hypotensive (systolic 82–95 mmHg) without vaginal bleeding. This prompted an urgent MRI to map the location of the pregnancy.

cases.case_text:

Thoracentesis yielded an exudative, lymphocyte-predominant fluid with red color; stains and cultures were negative. A 66-year-old white man presented to the Emergency Department with abrupt onset of dyspnea, palpitations, and lightheadedness. In the ED, he was found to be in monomorphic ventricular tachycardia and was electrically cardioverted into normal sinus rhythm. His medical history included a cerebrovascular accident, Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutations, hypertension, incidentally noted pulmonary nodules, and chronic kidney disease (baseline GFR 40–45 mL/min/1.73 m2). He was taking losartan and warfarin and had no family history of sudden cardiac death.

Initial laboratory studies were within normal limits, and coronary angiography ruled out ischemia. His electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes, but an epsilon wave in V1, a QRS duration of 140 ms, and T-wave inversions in leads V1–V5. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed preserved left ventricular function and no valvular disease, but a markedly dilated right ventricle with severely reduced systolic function. Based on an epsilon wave in V1–V3, T-wave inversions in V1–V3 with QRS >110 ms, an RV outflow tract dimension >32 mm, and severe RV dilation and hypokinesia, arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia was highly suspected. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was indicated but not performed because of chronic kidney disease and patient preference. A septal endomyocardial biopsy was considered but deferred due to its low yield. Given the patient’s pulmonary nodules, cardiac sarcoidosis remained in the differential diagnosis.

cases.case_text:
A 62-year-old woman presented with 4 months of soreness, swelling, and limited movement of her right palm and wrist. Six months earlier, she had been stabbed by a fishbone. cases.case_text:
A 9-month-old spayed female Ragdoll cat was evaluated for 5 days of persistent vomiting and one episode of hematemesis, along with reduced appetite and lethargy. The cat’s history was unremarkable; it had been fed a raw rabbit–based raw food (BARF) diet for 3 months. On examination, the cat was moderately dehydrated (≈7%), febrile (39.9°C), with pale mucous membranes (capillary refill time ~3 s) and mild discomfort on abdominal palpation; body condition score was 4/9 (4.2 kg). Complete blood count, serum biochemistry, and FIV/FeLV tests were within normal limits or negative. Thoracic and abdominal radiographs were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound revealed multiple rounded, echogenic neoformations at the pyloric antrum and mild mesenteric lymphadenomegaly; the remainder of the abdomen appeared normal. Intravenous fluids and omeprazole were initiated. Endoscopy showed several sessile, smooth-surfaced nodules (0.5–2 cm) in the pyloric antrum; the duodenum was normal. Cytological brushing of the gastric mucosa demonstrated mucosal cells, mixed neutrophilic and macrophagic inflammation, and occasional large, non-septate hyphae with irregular diameter and branching. A 51-year-old woman with a history of gastric adenocarcinoma—treated with neoadjuvant FLOT chemotherapy, gastrectomy, and adjuvant FLOT—was found one year later to have metastatic lesions in the liver, pancreas, left adrenal gland, para-aortic lymph nodes, and a lytic bone lesion in the left iliac bone. She received palliative radiotherapy (20 Gy in 4 fractions) to the L4 vertebra for back pain. On follow-up, she appeared ill but was hemodynamically stable (normal vital signs) with an ECOG performance status of 2. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable; the abdomen was soft, with a palpable liver and well-healed surgical scars. A peripheral blood smear showed scattered red blood cell fragments (schistocytes) among normal red blood cells. Direct and indirect Coombs tests were negative. Laboratory results: hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL, hematocrit 23.4%, MCV 85 fL, RBC count 2.76 × 10^6/μL, platelets 22.3 × 10^3/μL, total bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, indirect bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, haptoglobin 0.0 mg/dL, LDH 1621 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 1669 U/L, PT 19 s, PTT 28.1 s, fibrinogen 208 mg/dL, INR 1.24, creatinine 0.5 mg/dL. Her PLASMIC score was 6 (high).

A. Cancer associated microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
B. TTP was considered but excluded due to absence of neurologic signs
C. HUS was deemed unlikely given normal renal function
D. DIC was ruled out because of normal fibrinogen levels and no prolongation of PT or PTT

annotation.title: Neonatal scrotal wall necrotizing fasciitis (Fournier gangrene): a case report

cases.case_text:
A 10-day-old full-term boy was admitted with viral gastroenteritis, when pediatric surgery was consulted for left scrotal swelling. A left hydrocele was diagnosed, and he was discharged. Seventeen days later, at four weeks of age, he returned with a 24-hour history of left scrotal swelling, erythema, fever, and a pus-like discharge from an ulcerated area of the left hemi-scrotum. Abdominal examination was normal. Scrotal examination revealed a left scrotal abscess with a hard, swollen left testis; no hernia was identified. A provisional diagnosis of missed neonatal testicular torsion was made, and the baby was prepared for immediate surgical exploration. Intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate and flucloxacillin and fluids were started in light of the local scrotal infection.

annotation.title: Slowly progressive invasive rhino‐orbito‐cerebral aspergillosis: case report and literature review

cases.case_text:
A 65-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of a slowly progressive orbital mass causing left exophthalmia, left hemifacial pain, and progressive visual impairment culminating in total vision loss.  
Her medical history included 8 years of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, stage IIB cervical adenocarcinoma treated 3 years earlier with concurrent radiotherapy and weekly cisplatin, and well-controlled hypertension, dyslipidemia, and hypothyroidism.  
On examination, she had left exophthalmia with vision impairment and complete restriction of ocular motility. Anterior rhinoscopy, oral cavity, and neck examinations were unremarkable; nasofibrolaryngoscopy revealed a discrete medial bulging of the left nasal fossa lateral wall and a leftward septal deviation.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbital region showed a soft-tissue density lesion occupying the left maxillary sinus with extension into the orbit, ethmoidal and sphenoid sinuses, and bone discontinuity of the maxillary, septal, sphenoid, ethmoidal walls, and pterygopalatine fossa. MRI demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing mass in the left maxillary sinus, nasal cavity, ethmoidal sinuses, and intraorbital region, with bone disruption of the lateral and inferior orbital walls, extension through the inferior orbital fissure, invasion of the left cavernous sinus, diffusion restriction around the ophthalmic nerve, and anterior displacement of the extraocular muscles and vessels; these findings were considered highly suggestive of malignant neoplasm.  
Laboratory studies on admission showed HbA1c 8.8%, CRP 15.5 mg/L, ESR 120 mm/h, negative Cryptococcus antigen, nonreactive FTA-ABS, HIV, and hepatitis panels except positive anti-HBc, and CSF analysis with protein 58 mg/dL, glucose 66 mg/dL, WBC 5/mm3, IgG 11.3 mg/dL, negative cytology and cultures, and ADA 1.8 U/L.  
An endoscopic endonasal biopsy of the left maxillary sinus revealed on frozen section a probable low-grade lymphoproliferative lesion, but paraffin-fixed sections showed nonspecific chronic fibrosing inflammation without evidence of neoplasia, granulomas, or fungi.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Chronic invasive fungal rhinosinusitis
B. Malignant neoplasm
C. Low
D. Chronic nonspecific inflammatory process
E. Aspergilloma
F. Other nasal sinus neoplasms
G. Mucormycosis
H. None

annotation.title: Primary Pleuropulmonary Synovial Sarcoma: A Case

cases.case_text:
A 40-year-old woman, one month postpartum, with no significant past medical history, presented with three weeks of left chest pain, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea (mMRC grade III) in a context of general health deterioration. On examination, she had signs of a left pleural effusion. A posteroanterior chest radiograph showed a homogeneous opacity occupying the entire left hemithorax with mediastinal shift to the right. Serial thoracenteses produced approximately 2 L of serous fluid every three days. Thoracic ultrasonography confirmed a large pleural effusion; an ultrasound-guided pleural biopsy was non‐diagnostic. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 104 × 102 × 141 mm mediastino-pulmonary mass in the left upper lobe contacting the subclavian artery and lateral border of the aorta and encasing a branch of the left pulmonary artery, with a large ipsilateral pleural effusion. Bronchoscopic examination showed an endobronchial lesion in the left upper-lobe bronchus, but endobronchial biopsies were non‐contributory on two occasions.

annotation.title: Isolated arteritis misdiagnosed as bilateral orbital tumors in a patient with acute ischemic stroke

cases.case_text:
An 89-year-old woman with persistent atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) and hypertension presented with acute speech disturbance and right-sided weakness. On examination she was alert, had global aphasia, right facial asymmetry, right upper- and lower-limb paresis with decreased tone, and a right Babinski sign; NIH Stroke Scale score was 19. She had no history of COVID-19, and two mRNA vaccine doses; RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 on admission and hospital day 3 was negative. 

Noncontrast head CT showed early ischemic changes in the left insula and frontal lobe. CT angiography revealed acute occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery at M1/M2 and chronic occlusion of the left internal carotid artery; an incidental mass in the left orbit was also noted. She received intravenous thrombolysis with reperfusion of the left ICA. Conventional angiography confirmed left MCA occlusion and restored flow in the ICA and ACA. Mechanical thrombectomy achieved angiographic reperfusion of the MCA but no clinical improvement; follow-up CT confirmed an infarct in the left MCA territory. 

Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral oval lesions in the medial orbits, which were initially interpreted as orbital tumors. CT angiography of the chest showed pulmonary emboli in segmental arteries of the right lower lobe. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, degenerative mitral and aortic valves, and severe low-gradient aortic stenosis with preserved ejection fraction. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring confirmed atrial fibrillation; ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was normal. 

Laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein (10.74 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (0.11 ng/mL) with normal renal, liver function, and electrolytes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild pleocytosis (10 cells/µL) and elevated protein (55 mg/dL) with normal glucose. Multiple blood and urine cultures were negative, and repeat SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative. Vasculitic, autoimmune, viral infection, and malignancy screens were unremarkable, and rheumatology and angiology consultations excluded systemic vasculitis, neoplasm, and histiocytosis.

annotation.title: Acute Liver Failure Due to Budd-Chiari Syndrome in the Setting of Cardiac Synovial Sarcoma

cases.case_text:
A 60-year-old man with hypertension and Parkinson’s disease presented with 3 months of progressive lower extremity edema and acute onset of altered mental status. On admission, he was somnolent and disoriented; examination showed symmetric lower extremity edema, hepatomegaly, and ascites without stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory tests revealed AST 3877 U/L, ALT 2939 U/L, total bilirubin 4.5 mg/dL, INR 3.8, white blood cell count 19.4×10^3/μL, platelets 63×10^3/μL, lactic acid 13.9 mmol/L, BUN 67 mg/dL, creatinine 3.3 mg/dL, with a negative acetaminophen level and toxicology screen. Viral hepatitis panels, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and HIV testing were negative. A diagnostic paracentesis was negative for infection or malignancy. Tests for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, hemochromatosis, and Wilson’s disease were unremarkable. The patient developed hepatorenal syndrome requiring continuous venovenous hemofiltration.  
Lower-extremity Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated extensive bilateral femoral–popliteal and iliac vein thrombosis. IVC filter placement was aborted due to clot burden. Hepatic ultrasonography with Doppler showed hepatic vein thrombosis and reversal of portal venous flow. Contrast CT of the abdomen, thorax, and pelvis revealed thrombus extending into the right atrium. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a large echodense mass in the right atrium with preserved left ventricular function. Cardiac MRI demonstrated a 10.6×5.0×5.6-cm heterogeneous pericardial mass invading the right atrium.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Synovial sarcoma
B. thrombophilic and myeloproliferative causes
C. Atrial myxoma as a benign cardiac tumor causing BCS
D. Caval rhabdomyosarcoma as a malignant cause of BCS
E. Primary cardiac adenocarcinoma as another neoplastic cause of hepatic vein obstruction

cases.case_text:
A 12-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a facial angioma. MRI of the brain showed no leptomeningeal vascular malformations. Examination revealed bilateral naevus flammeus along the ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of the trigeminal nerve, more extensive on the right. Visual acuity was 20/20 in each eye. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye showed iris heterochromia with diffuse hyperpigmentation and evenly distributed micronodular elevations on the iris surface. Intraocular pressure measured by Icare tonometry was 22 mm Hg in the right eye and 12 mm Hg in the left. Gonioscopy demonstrated open angles bilaterally with diffuse trabecular hyperpigmentation in the right eye. Anterior-segment OCT revealed increased reflectance of the iris surface in the right eye. Funduscopic examination showed increased retinal vessel tortuosity and a diffusely darker fundus in the right eye. B-scan ultrasonography measured choroidal thickness of 2.2 mm in the right eye versus 1.4 mm in the left. Macular spectral-domain OCT confirmed a thicker choroid in the right eye. annotation.title: Adrenal extramedullary hematopoiesis associated with beta-thalassemia trait in an adult woman: a case report and review of literature

cases.case_text:
A 48-year-old Pakistani woman presented with a 2-year history of intermittent vomiting, right upper-quadrant pain, and a sensation of fullness on the right side of the abdomen. She denied urinary symptoms or changes in bowel habits. Her medical history was notable for heavy menstruation and iron deficiency anemia managed with oral iron for over 10 years. On examination, there was fullness of the right upper quadrant with a large, firm, palpable mass with a rounded surface and ill-defined borders. annotation.title: Multiple plexiform schwannomas in the plantar aspect of the foot: case report and literature review

cases.case_text:
A 19-year-old woman presented with an 18-month history of pain in the plantar aspect of her left foot.  The pain was moderate initially, often worse at night, and markedly exacerbated by compression and exposure to cold.  Over the past four months, the patient noted aggravation of the local pain and was referred for imaging.  She denied any trauma and had no family history of neurofibromatosis.  

On examination, three prominent, soft-tissue nodules with swelling and tenderness were palpated in the plantar aspect of the left foot; they were mobile and not adherent to surrounding tissue.  Sensation testing revealed numbness in the medial distal plantar foot; toe and foot motor strength were normal.  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left foot demonstrated three nodules arranged in a linear distribution in the mid-plantar region.  On T1-weighted images, the lesions were homogeneously isointense to skeletal muscle.  On T2-weighted fat-suppressed images, they were homogeneously hyperintense without cystic degeneration; each was surrounded by a hyperintense rim.  A small extension of high signal from the lateral aspect of one lesion resembled a “mouse-tail.”  Two nodules were located within the flexor digitorum brevis muscle beneath the plantar aponeurosis, and one was in the superficial fascia at the third metatarsophalangeal joint.  The lesions followed the course of branches of the common plantar digital nerves without evidence of invasion.

A 50-year-old man with a remote history of treated Lyme disease, and no hypertension, hyperlipidemia, or diabetes, presented after four episodes of syncope over 24 hours. Six weeks earlier, he had a syncope while exercising; initial workup was unrevealing. Outpatient ECG then showed a new left bundle branch block. Exercise stress testing provoked presyncope with a brief burst of atrial tachycardia. A pharmacological nuclear stress test demonstrated an LVEF of 42% with a moderate-size area of inferior wall ischaemia and scar, but he had no chest pain or heart failure symptoms.

On current presentation, vital signs were blood pressure 140/66 mmHg, heart rate 54 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 36.2°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. He had a brief burst of atrial tachycardia that resolved with IV metoprolol. Cardiac enzymes, thyroid function tests, serum calcium, and ACE levels were normal. Lyme antibody testing was negative. Her history included heavy menstrual bleeding, a miscarriage at age 14, chronic warfarin-refractory deep vein thromboses, and placement of a nonretrievable inferior vena cava filter. She denied fevers, chills, or intravenous drug use.

On examination she was obese and mildly tachypneic, sitting forward. Vital signs: temperature 98.6°F, blood pressure 116/91 mm Hg, heart rate 88/min, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She had a malar rash, jugular venous distension, tender anterior chest wall, bibasilar Velcro crackles, and a grade 2/6 pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border that increased with inspiration.

A male infant was delivered at 34 weeks’ gestation by cesarean section for fetal growth restriction and oligohydramnios. He was admitted to the NICU, where echocardiography showed a restrictive ventricular septal defect, a wide patent foramen ovale, and a small secundum atrial septal defect with left-to-right shunt. Beginning on day 11, he developed progressive respiratory failure requiring supplemental oxygen, bronchodilators, and diuretics. cases.case_text:
A 19-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 2-week history of progressive headache and two episodes of vomiting. His parents also noted a 12-month history of apathy and declining academic performance. On neurologic examination, he had a right pronator drift; the remainder of his examination was normal. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed a large extra-axial heterogeneous mass over the left frontal and temporal convexity with well-defined lobulated margins and avid enhancement of denser areas; there was erosion of the inner table of the left frontal bone and near-complete erosion of the outer table. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated a 6.2×7.1×7.0 cm extra-axial ovoid mass at the left frontal convexity with heterogeneous enhancement and susceptibility artifacts consistent with calcification and/or hemorrhage. cases.case_text:
A 36-year-old woman presented with a 7-day history of right-sided chest pain and dyspnea without fever or cough. She reported two prior spontaneous pneumothoraces: one right-sided in 2018 managed medically, and one left-sided in 2019 treated surgically. She also noted occasional small-volume hemoptysis. 

On admission, she was alert, with SpO2 97% on room air. Right chest auscultation revealed hypoventilation; no crackles were appreciated. The remainder of the examination, including endocrine and genitourinary systems, was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies (CBC, chemistry, urinalysis) were within normal limits; microbiological tests for tuberculosis and other bacteria were negative. 

Chest radiography showed lung hyperinflation without focal parenchymal abnormalities. HRCT of the chest revealed a small right pneumothorax and numerous round, thin-walled air cysts (2–5 mm) scattered in both lungs; no irregular cyst shapes were noted. 

Pulmonary function testing demonstrated a 6-minute walk distance of 67% predicted, normal DLCO, and a negative bronchodilator response. 

Thirteen days later, she developed left-sided chest pain and dyspnea. Chest X-ray confirmed a new left pneumothorax; CT again showed a large left pneumothorax with passive atelectasis and persistent small air cysts bilaterally. Thoracoscopic surgery with pleural drainage was performed, and lung biopsies were obtained.

A 45-year-old man with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus, well controlled without immunomodulatory therapy, presented with a 30 × 20 mm painless, slowly progressive mass on his left forehead over 1 year. He had undergone excision of a similar frontal bone lesion diagnosed as fibrous dysplasia 2 years earlier. He denied headaches or neurologic symptoms.  
On CT scan, the lesion showed a ground-glass appearance with homogenous matrix expansion of the frontal bone, predominantly affecting the external cortex. Fine-needle aspiration cytology with immunostaining excluded multiple myeloma (no CD138+ cells). cases.case_text:
A 96-year-old man with benign prostatic disease and dementia presented after a collapse at home. On admission, he had normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 119 g/L), a D-dimer of 1095 ng/mL, normal troponin, normal C-reactive protein, and neutrophilia (10.44 × 10^9/L). A diagnosis of venous thromboembolism was considered but excluded on the basis of Well’s score, and he was discharged with antibiotics for a presumed urinary tract infection. The next day, he returned with a swollen right knee and thigh and extensive bruising, findings that were suspicious for deep vein thrombosis. Lower limb ultrasound showed a patent venous system and identified a 45 mm popliteal artery aneurysm with an 11.4 × 5.2 cm medial leg hematoma. Seven days later, he was admitted emergently with worsening right-leg pain and difficulty walking. Examination revealed extensive bruising behind the right knee and posterior-medial thigh, a pulsatile mass extending into the mid-thigh, and a pulseless right foot without signs of acute ischemia. Repeat hemoglobin was 77 g/L. A 4-day-old Asian Chinese female newborn was referred for evaluation of multiple masses protruding from her gums that interfered with feeding. cases.case_text:
An 80-year-old woman was referred for management of a chronic superficial sacral wound present for approximately 2 years. She reported progressively worsening sacral pain and local skin irritation but denied purulent discharge, altered bowel habits, rectal bleeding, or rectal discharge. Her history was notable for inverse psoriasis affecting the natal cleft, prior coccygectomy 20 years earlier, multiple cutaneous nonmelanoma skin cancers, ischemic heart disease status post coronary artery bypass grafting, hypertension, dyslipidemia, mild asthma, and splenectomy. Medications included aspirin, rosuvastatin, valsartan, and topical corticosteroids as needed.

On examination, she was afebrile and systemically well. The coccygectomy scar was slightly indurated and surrounded by a broad area of excoriated skin with plaques and focal ulceration in the upper natal cleft. A small superior sinus tract without obvious pits and mild serous discharge were noted. The lesion was located more than 5 cm from the anal verge. There was no exophytic mass, no underlying abscess cavity, and no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy.

annotation.title: A Case of Overlap Syndrome of Systemic Sclerosis and Cryoglobulinemic Vasculitis With Central Nervous System Involvement

cases.case_text:
A 41-year-old woman with a 3-year history of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis presented with the sudden onset of visual disturbances. At the time of her SSc diagnosis, she had skin sclerosis of the fingers, hands, forearms, and face, Raynaud’s phenomenon with digital ulcers, multiple facial telangiectasias, esophageal reflux, and interstitial lung disease. Nail-fold capillaroscopy showed capillary loss with dilatation and microhemorrhages. A forearm skin biopsy demonstrated increased dermal collagen and superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltration. Laboratory studies revealed a positive antinuclear antibody titer (>1:320) with a nucleolar pattern, negative anti-centromere antibody, and negative anti-Scl-70 antibody. She was treated with bosentan and aspirin, with stable pulmonary findings over two years.

Seven days before transfer, she was admitted elsewhere for fever over 38°C and headache. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed protein 161.6 mg/dL, glucose 39 mg/dL, red blood cells 0 /mm3, and white blood cells 459 /mm3 (88% polymorphonuclear cells). Serum C-reactive protein was 10.6 mg/dL and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 82 mm/h. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated T2 hyperintense lesions in the frontal, left parietal, and left occipital lobes with leptomeningeal enhancement. Empirical ceftriaxone and vancomycin were initiated. After four days, she developed visual disturbances; repeat MRI showed increased size and number of multifocal T2 hyperintense lesions along both cerebral hemispheres and midbrain, including a 4.5-cm lesion in the right posterior lobe. Tests of CSF—including Gram stain and culture, PCR for herpes simplex virus and enteroviruses, cryptococcal antigen, and fungal cultures—were negative. She was then referred to our hospital.

On arrival, she could only count fingers at close range and also reported headache, dizziness, fever, myalgia, polyarthralgia, and bilateral foot tingling. Blood pressure was 192/103 mmHg, heart rate 48 beats/min, and temperature 37.3°C. Electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia. Neurologic examination revealed drowsiness, neck stiffness, symmetrical proximal and distal weakness (muscle strength 4/5), paresthesia in both feet, brisk biceps reflexes, absent patellar reflexes, and bilaterally positive Babinski signs. A 4 × 5 cm ulcer was noted over the right lateral malleolus; there was no synovitis. The white-cell count was 14,090 /mm3, C-reactive protein was 3.09 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 56 mm/h. She continued antibiotics, and intravenous acyclovir, nicardipine, mannitol, and dexamethasone were added. Blood pressure stabilized within six hours, but her visual impairment worsened, and she developed left-sided weakness and new Raynaud’s phenomenon in her fingers. Emergent cerebral angiography revealed diffuse stenosis and a beaded pattern of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries and their branches, along with diffuse luminal narrowing and dysplastic changes in the right distal vertebral artery and basilar trunk, consistent with cerebral angiitis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. cryoglobulinemic vasculitis
B. Bacterial meningitis
C. Viral encephalitis
D. Cryptococcal or fungal meningitis
E. Lymphoproliferative disorder
F. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES)
G. None

cases.case_text:
A 35-year-old woman presented with neck pain after a motor vehicle accident. She had a 15-year history of migraine headaches; over the past year they had become more severe and positional (worse when lying down). She also reported 3 months of memory impairment and dizziness, and 1 year of gradual-onset tinnitus and dysphagia. Physical examination was unremarkable. 

Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a mass in the left cerebellomedullary cistern isodense to gray matter without calcifications. CT angiography showed displacement of the prepontine vessels without encasement. MRI demonstrated a 3.4×3.3×3.3 cm, well-circumscribed mass in the left cerebellomedullary and premedullary cisterns that was hyperintense to CSF on T1- and T2-weighted images, did not restrict diffusion, showed a focus of susceptibility-related signal loss, had no enhancement, and exerted mass effect on the brainstem and cerebellum without surrounding edema.

C. Choroid plexus cyst
D. Ependymal cyst
E. Epidermoid/dermoid cyst
